Inter-coder reliability is a continuation of the coding practice process because it determines how similar independent coders evaluate a characteristic of the same message and reach the same conclusion [@tinsley2000] <a href="/resources/papers/tinsley2000.pdf" target = "_blank"> <img src="download-icon.png" alt="Tinsley and Weiss (2000)" width="20" height="20"></a> . Therefore, the target of coding practice is to achieve as high inter-coder reliability as possible.

## Coding protocol

Coding potocol has been previously discussed in this book, but I think it is important to highlight it because this is a source of low inter-coder reliability level. This is especially the case when the coding process and inter-coder reliability are calculated in the QDA software such as NVIVO, ATLAS.ti, and Taguette. These softwares cannot interprete meaning of the coded sentences, and thus coding different sentence even with the same meaning will be considered "disagreement".

Coding protocol should cover what to find, where to look, what to code. First, to make it easier, research questions can be broken down into subquestions, so it will be easier for the coders to find the information for each part of the research question. Similarly, the codebook can be assigned for each part of the research question. Second, the coding protocol should specify which parts of the article should be coded. For example, the research result can be found in abstract, finding, discussion, and conclusion sections. Therefore, to ensure that each coder code in the same section, the coding protocol should specify which section of the article to prioritize and whether another section needs to be considered when the information is not found in the prioritized section.

## Sample size and selection

There is no consensus on the number of articles or interviews to code for for inter-coder reliability purpose. @oconnor2020 <a href="/resources/papers/oconnor2020.pdf" target = "_blank"> <img src="download-icon.png" alt="O’Connor and Joffe (2022)" width="20" height="20"></a> propose a subset of 10-25% of papers or interviews, depending on the size of the data, but I also rarely found any papers reporting more than ten papers for inter-coder reliability. In my projects, I always use 10% with a maximum of 10 papers or interviews.

Regarding the selection process of articles or interviews for inter-coder reliability purpose, @oconnor2020 <a href="/resources/papers/oconnor2020.pdf" target = "_blank"> <img src="download-icon.png" alt="O’Connor and Joffe (2022)" width="20" height="20"></a> propose that these papers are selected randomly. When there are two research questions and each research question consists of different papers, the same number of articles for each research question should be randomly selected. The random selection ensures that the selected papers represents all papers in the project.

## Codebook preparation

When the inter-coder reliability is calculated using QDA software, all coders need to use the same codebook. Therefore, a file needs to be prepared by one coder to be distributed to the others. Upon receiving the file, the user in the file needs to be resetted and set to the current coder. Otherwise, some QDA softwares such as NVIVO, will not be able to display the inter-coder reliability level accurately. These files are later merged to calculate the inter-coder reliability level. Each QDA software has a detailed instruction on how to show the inter-coder reliability. In our coding demonstration, we will use Taguette because it is an open source application, accessed remotely (<a href="https://app.taguette.org" target = "_blank" style="text-decoration:none">https://app.taguette.org</a>). In this software, one codebook prepared by one coder, and then this coder can invite the other coders to work on the same codebook.

When the intercoder reliability is calculated manually, the codebook preparation can be more flexible because the data will be moved manually to a spreadsheet and manually assessed for meaning. However, moving this data is much easier when the files can me merged and a record of "who codes which" is available.

## Coding process

After the codebook is prepared, each coder work independently. During this process, the team should have a venue to keep discussing about the codebook and coding protocol because there should not be any confusion during this process. In my cases, my team discussed through WhatApp group and had weekly online meeting, which run from the start to the end of the project. 

## Calculating inter-coder reliability in QDA software

After completing this coding process, depending on the QDA software you use, all files may need to be merged. When we used an online QDA software which enables collaboration, the inter-coder reliability may be calculated immediately. 

In NVIVO, the files are merged by importing project, where the project is the file coded by another coder. This feature can be accessed from "Import" and select "Project." Later, we need to choose "merge" in the option. 




## Calculating inter-coder reliability manually
One of the shortcomings in using QDA software to calculate inter-coder reliability is that this software cannot determine "agreement" and "disagreement" based on meaning. Therefore, when two coders code a different sentence in a text, the software consider it as "disagreement" even when the meaning is similar. In this section, I will replicate the calculation of inter-coder reliability using Cohen's Kappa coefficient in NVIVO outside the software. The Cohen's Kappa calculation used to calculate the intercoder reliabilty in NVIVO is different to the conventional calculation because NVIVO include disagreement in the calculation. For demonstration, we will use the following data.

```{=html}
<embed src="/resources/pdf_images/icr_data.pdf" width="800px" height="300px" />
```

The formula to calculate Cohen's Kappa for the inter-coder reliability is similar to the formula we used in determining reliability in abstract screening.
$$ \kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e} $$

To use this formula, we will need the following details:
<ol>
    <li> Total number of sentences in all coded articles/intervierws</li>
    <li> Number of sentences coded by both Coder A and Coder B</li>
    <li> Number of sentences coded by Coder A only </li>
    <li> Number of sentences coded by Coder B only </li>
    <li> Number of sentences NOT coded by Coder A </li>
    <li> Number of sentences NOT coded by Coder B </li>
    <li> Number of sentences NOT coded by either Coder A and Coder B </li>
</ol>

### Step 1. Total number of sentences

The total number of sentences is calculated by adding the number of sentences in all papers coded for the inter-coder reliability purpose.

```{r cache = TRUE}
icr_data <- data.frame(Article_ID = c(paste0("Article_", 1:7), "Article_9", "Article_10"),
                         No_of_sentences = c(435, 467, 472, 412, 511, 457, 481, 502, 400))
icr_data
sum(icr_data$No_of_sentences)                       
```
Based on the calculation, the total number of sentences is `4,137`.

### Step 2. Number of sentences not coded

Number of sentences not coded by Coder A is calculated using this formula:

$$ \text{Coder } A^- = \text{Total} - (\text{Coder A and Coder B} + \text{Coder A only}) $$
$$ \text{Coder } A^- = 4,137 - (12 + 7) = 4,118 $$

Number of sentences not coded by Coder B is calculated using this formula:

$$ \text{Coder } B^- = \text{Total} - (\text{Coder A and Coder B} + \text{Coder B only}) $$
$$ \text{Coder } B^- = 4,137 - (12 + 4) = 4,121 $$

Number of sentences not coded by either Coder A and Coder B is calculated using this formula:
$$ \text{Coder } A^- \text{and } B^-= \text{Total} - (\text{Coder A and B} + \text{Coder A only} + \text{Coder B only}) $$
$$ \text{Coder } A^- \text{and } B^-= 4,137 - (12 + 7 + 4) = 4,114 $$

### Step 3. Breaking down NVIVO Cohen's Kappa coefficient

The Cohen's Kappa coefficient, as shown above, requires calculation of P<sub>o</sub> and P<sub>e</sub>. The formula for these variables are given below.

$$ P_o = \frac{\text{Coder} A \text{ and } B + \text{Coder } A^- \text{ or } B^-}{\text{Total}} = \frac{12 + 4,114}{4,137} = 0.997$$

Meanwhile, the formula to calculate P<sub>e</sub> requires the calculation of some probabilities.
$$ P_e = (P_A x P_B) + (P_A^- x B_B^-)$$

Where:
<ul>
    <li> P<sub>A</sub> = The probability that only Coder A would code </li>
    <li> P<sub>B</sub> = The probability that only Coder B would code </li>
    <li>P<sub>A</sub><sup>--</sup> = The probability that only coder A would not code </li>
    <li>P<sub>B</sub><sup>--</sup> = The probability that only coder B would not code </li>
</ul>

The formula and calculation of these variables as as follows:

$$P_A = \frac{\text{Coder} A \text{ and } B + \text{Coder } A} {\text{Total}} = \frac{12 + 7}{4,137} = 0.00459$$

$$P_B = \frac{\text{Coder} A \text{ and } B + \text{Coder } B} {\text{Total}} = \frac{12 + 4}{4,137} = 0.00387$$

$$P_A^- = \frac{\text{Coder} A^-} {\text{Total}} = \frac{4,118}{4,137} = 0.995$$

$$P_B^- = \frac{\text{Coder} B^-} {\text{Total}} = \frac{4,121}{4,137} = 0.996$$

Using the results above, P<sub>e</sub> can now be calculated:

$$ P_e = (P_A x P_B) + (P_A^- x B_B^-) = (0.00459 x 0.00387) + (0.995 x 0.996) = 0.991$$

Finally, the Cohen's Kappa can be calculated:

$$ \kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e} = \frac{0.997 - 0.991} {1 - 0.991} = 0.667$$
